43906: Creation, the Egyptian plague, Sinai's thick darkness, and the prophets' day of the LORD.
43907: Darkness covers the land at Jesus' death; John's Gospel contrasts light and darkness; Paul describes conversion as moving from darkness to light (Acts 26:18).
43908: Darkness in Scripture is never about skin colour. Using 'dark' and 'light' imagery to rank peoples is a misuse of these texts that has caused real harm. Christian mystics (for example the tradition behind *The Cloud of Unknowing*) also use darkness positively for God's mystery.
43910: Clouds both reveal and hide. In the Bible a cloud often shows that God is present while veiling his full glory. It guided Israel in the desert, filled the temple, and appears when Jesus is transfigured and ascends.
43912: Israel moved when the cloud moved and stopped when it stopped.
43914: The cloud filled the tabernacle and temple so that priests could not stand to minister.
43915: The Father's voice at the transfiguration
43916: A bright cloud overshadows the disciples and the Father speaks.
43917: The Son of Man coming with clouds
43918: In Daniel the Son of Man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days. Some read Jesus' use of this as his vindication and enthronement (fulfilled at the resurrection, ascension and the fall of Jerusalem); others read it of his visible return. Many hold both.
43920: The faithful of Hebrews 11 surround believers like a cloud.
43921: The pillar of cloud, Sinai's cloud, the temple cloud, and clouds as God's chariot (Ps 104:3). Paul says Israel was 'baptised in the cloud and in the sea' (1 Cor 10:2).
43922: Transfiguration, ascension and return all involve clouds, linking Jesus to the Old Testament glory-cloud.
43923: The later Jewish term Shekinah (God's 'dwelling' presence) is often used for the glory-cloud, but the word itself does not appear in the Bible; it comes from rabbinic writings.
43925: In both Hebrew and Greek the same word can mean wind, breath or spirit. So the invisible moving air becomes a picture of God's life-giving Spirit: unseen, powerful, and the source of life.
43926: The breath of life from God
43927: God breathes life into Adam; when he takes away breath, creatures die.
43929: In Ezekiel's valley of dry bones the breath, wind and Spirit are one word. Jesus breathes on the disciples; Pentecost comes as a rushing wind.
43931: God parts the sea with wind and sends wind to bring quail; Jesus rebukes the wind.
43933: Human life is a breath; much effort is 'chasing the wind'.
43935: The four winds mean all directions.
43936: Ruach appears hundreds of times for wind, human spirit and God's Spirit. The Spirit comes on judges, kings and prophets for specific tasks.
43937: Pneuma is the regular word for the Holy Spirit. Jesus plays on the double meaning when he tells Nicodemus the wind blows where it wishes.
43938: In Genesis 1:2 ruach elohim can be translated 'Spirit of God', 'wind from God' or even 'mighty wind'; translations differ, and readers should not build too much on one rendering.
43941: Israel depended on rain, not on a great river like Egypt's Nile. Timely rain and morning dew meant crops and life; drought meant famine. So rain and dew became pictures of God's blessing, his word and his Spirit.
43943: Faithfulness brings rain in season; Elijah's drought confronts Baal, the supposed storm god.
43945: God's word falls like rain and does not return without effect.
43947: Joel moves from the early and latter rain to the Spirit poured on all people.
43949: God sends rain on the just and unjust; this is often called common grace.
43951: Gideon's fleece and the dew of Hermon.
43952: The early (autumn) and latter (spring) rains framed the farming year. Rain at the wrong time could be a sign of judgement (1 Sam 12:17-18), and the flood is rain as destruction.
43953: James uses Elijah's prayer for rain as an example of effective prayer (Jas 5:17-18) and the farmer waiting for rains as a picture of patience (Jas 5:7).
43954: The 'Latter Rain' movement (1940s onward) took Joel 2:23 as a prophecy of an end-time revival with restored apostles and prophets; most interpreters read Joel's rains first as literal harvest rains that picture the Spirit's coming at Pentecost. See /movements/prophetic-movement.
43956: Israel was not a seafaring nation, and the sea seemed restless, dangerous and untamed. In the Bible it often stands for chaos and hostile powers that only God can master. In the new creation 'there is no more sea'.
43958: God sets limits to the sea and crushes the sea monster Leviathan or Rahab.
43960: God parts the Red Sea; Jesus calms the storm and walks on the water, doing what the Old Testament says God does.
43961: Restless nations and the source of evil empires
43962: Beasts representing empires rise from the sea.
43963: Chaos removed in the new creation
43964: 'No more sea' probably means no more chaos, danger or separation, not literally no oceans; readers differ.
43965: Creation, the Red Sea crossing, Jonah's storm, and the great bronze 'sea' basin in Solomon's temple (1 Kgs 7:23-26).
43966: Jesus' stilling of the storm and walking on water; Revelation's sea of glass before God's throne (Rev 4:6; Rev 15:2) shows chaos made calm.
43967: Neighbouring cultures told myths of gods fighting the sea (Baal against Yam in Ugaritic texts; Marduk against Tiamat in Babylon). Scholars broadly agree the Bible uses similar imagery while insisting there is one God and the sea is his creature, not a rival god; how much was borrowed is debated.
43969: Rivers bring water to dry land and make life possible. The Bible begins with a river flowing out of Eden and ends with the river of the water of life flowing from God's throne.
43971: Ezekiel's river flows from the temple and makes the Dead Sea fresh; Revelation's river flows from the throne.
43973: Rivers of living water flow from the believer's heart, which John explains as the Spirit.
43977: The Euphrates marked the edge of the promised land and, in Revelation, a frontier from which judgement comes.
43978: The Nile (Egypt's life source, turned to blood in the first plague), the Euphrates, the Jordan, and the rivers of Babylon where the exiles wept (Ps 137:1).
43979: Baptism in the Jordan, Lydia's conversion by a riverside place of prayer (Acts 16:13), and the river of life.
43984: A rock is solid, unmoving and a safe high place to hide. 'Rock' is one of the Bible's favourite names for God: dependable, a refuge, a foundation.
43985: God as rock: faithful and dependable
43986: Moses' song repeatedly names God 'the Rock'.
43988: Paul says 'the rock was Christ', reading the wilderness event as pointing to Christ.
43990: Hearing and doing Jesus' words is building on rock.
43991: 'On this rock I will build my church'
43992: The rock is Peter himself (Catholic view, and many Protestant scholars today); Peter's confession of faith (common among Reformers and some Fathers); or Christ himself (also an ancient reading). Debated.
43994: The same rock that saves trips up those who refuse it.
43995: God hides Moses in a cleft of the rock as his glory passes (Exod 33:21-22). David hides in rocky strongholds and names God his rock.
43996: Peter's name (Greek Petros, Aramaic Kephas) means 'rock'. Jesus' tomb was cut in rock (Mark 15:46).
43999: Mountains are high, hard to reach and close to the sky, so in the Bible they are where heaven and earth meet. God gives the law on a mountain, the temple stands on a mountain, and Jesus teaches, is transfigured and commissions his disciples on mountains.
44001: Moriah, Horeb/Sinai and Elijah's encounter on Horeb.
44002: Zion: God's dwelling and centre for the nations
44003: In the last days the LORD's mountain is raised above all others and the nations stream to it.
44005: Babylon is a 'destroying mountain'; God's kingdom becomes a mountain filling the earth.
44007: Matthew places key moments on mountains, echoing Moses at Sinai.
44009: A mountain becomes a plain before Zerubbabel; faith can move mountains.
44010: Ararat, Moriah, Sinai, Carmel, Zion. 'High places' on hills were also sites of idolatry that faithful kings tore down (2 Kgs 18:4).
44011: The Sermon on the Mount, the transfiguration, the Mount of Olives, and the great commission. Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that true worship is not tied to either mountain (John 4:20-24).
44012: The 'seven mountains' teaching (that Christians must take over seven spheres of culture) uses Isaiah 2:2 and Revelation 17:9 in ways most commentators consider foreign to their context. See /movements/dominion-theology.
44016: The wilderness is dry, empty land where people cannot survive on their own. In the Bible it is a place of testing and failure, but also of God's care and fresh beginnings, where he speaks to his people with nothing else to distract them.
44018: Israel was tested forty years; Jesus is tested forty days and succeeds where Israel failed.
44020: God feeds Israel with manna and Elijah with bread; Hosea pictures God wooing Israel in the desert like a bride.
44022: A generation died in the desert because of unbelief, a warning to later readers.
44023: The way of a new exodus
44024: The prophets foresee a highway through the desert for God's return; John the Baptist preaches there.
44026: The scapegoat carries Israel's sins into the wilderness.
44027: Hagar, Moses, Israel's wanderings, David hiding from Saul, and Elijah fleeing Jezebel all meet God in the wilderness.
44028: John the Baptist's ministry, Jesus' temptation, and his habit of withdrawing to deserted places to pray (Luke 5:16). The woman of Revelation 12 is protected in the wilderness.
44030: In a dry land a well-watered garden is a picture of delight, rest and plenty. The Bible begins in a garden, Jesus is arrested in a garden and buried in one, and the end of the story is a garden-city.
44032: God walks in the garden with the first humans.
44034: Some scholars (for example Gordon Wenham and G. K. Beale) note temple-like features: entrance from the east, cherubim guards, and the verbs 'serve and keep' also used of priests. Others think the parallels are overdrawn.
44036: God will make the wilderness like Eden and his people like a watered garden.
44038: The beloved is a locked garden; often read also of God and his people.
44040: The tree of life returns in the city of God.
44041: Eden, the king's garden, vineyards and the garden imagery of the prophets and the Song of Songs.
44042: Gethsemane (a garden, John 18:1); the tomb in a garden (John 19:41), where Mary mistakes the risen Jesus for the gardener (John 20:15), which many read as a deliberate new-creation echo.
44044: Many ancient peoples worshipped the sun, moon and stars as gods. Genesis calls them simply 'lights' made by God to mark time. In the Bible they also picture countless descendants, rulers and powers, and the shaking of the world when God judges.
44046: Genesis avoids even naming the sun and moon, perhaps to deny them divine status; worshipping them is forbidden.
44048: Abraham's offspring will be as many as the stars.
44050: Joseph's family appear as sun, moon and stars; a 'star out of Jacob' is a coming king; the seven stars are the angels of the churches.
44052: Sun darkened, moon turned to blood, stars falling. Isaiah uses this for Babylon's fall, which suggests it can be vivid language for the collapse of a political order; others expect literal cosmic events at the end. Debated.
44054: Christ is the bright morning star; the righteous will shine like stars.
44055: Creation, the promise to Abraham, Balaam's star oracle, the sun standing still for Joshua (Josh 10:12-13), and warnings against worshipping the 'host of heaven'.
44056: The Magi follow a star (Matt 2:2; Matt 2:9-10); the sun darkens at the crucifixion; Revelation's woman is clothed with the sun.
44057: The Bible forbids astrology as a way of reading the future (Isa 47:13-14). What the star of Bethlehem was (a miracle, a planetary conjunction, a comet or nova) is speculative.
44058: Egypt was the great power to Israel's south-west. In the Bible it is first a place of refuge and food, then the 'house of slavery' from which God rescued Israel. It becomes a picture of bondage, and of trusting in human power instead of God.
44060: God introduces himself as the one who brought Israel out of Egypt.
44062: Abraham, Jacob's family and the infant Jesus all find refuge there.
44063: God's son called out of Egypt
44064: Hosea is about Israel's exodus; Matthew sees Jesus relive Israel's story.
44065: Kings who ran to Egypt for military help are rebuked; Egypt is a broken reed.
44066: A spiritual condition and a future hope
44067: Revelation calls the city that killed the Lord 'spiritually Sodom and Egypt'; Isaiah astonishingly calls Egypt 'my people'.
44068: From Abraham's visit to Joseph's rise, the exodus, Solomon's marriage alliance and the prophets' warnings, Egypt is a constant presence.
44069: The holy family's flight, Stephen's retelling of the exodus (Acts 7), and Hebrews' picture of Moses choosing Christ's reproach over the treasures of Egypt (Heb 11:26).
44070: Later Christian writers used 'Egypt' for the sinful world or for slavery to sin, which is a fair extension of the exodus pattern but not a fixed code; in Isaiah 19 Egypt also receives a promise.
44071: Babylon was the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 586 BC and carried Judah into exile. Through the Bible it becomes a picture of proud human power that sets itself against God and oppresses his people.
44073: Babel's tower and Nebuchadnezzar's boast are humbled.
44074: Exile and God's instrument of judgement
44075: Babylon disciplines Judah, yet is itself judged after seventy years.
44076: Seeking the welfare of a foreign city
44077: Exiles are told to pray for Babylon's peace.
44078: The oppressive world power of the end
44079: Babylon the great is a seductive, wealthy, violent city that falls in one hour.
44081: Most scholars think Peter writes from Rome and Revelation's city on seven hills is Rome. Others suggest Jerusalem, a future city, or the world system in every age.
44082: Babel in Genesis, the exile in Kings and Chronicles, and oracles against Babylon in Isaiah and Jeremiah.
44083: Mentioned in Matthew's genealogy (Matt 1:11-12), as a code word in 1 Peter, and as the great city of Revelation 17 to 18.
44084: Many Reformers identified Revelation's Babylon with the papacy; this was a polemical reading of their time and is not held by most Protestant scholars today. Identifications with modern cities or nations are speculative.
44087: Jerusalem was David's capital and the site of the temple. Zion was first the hill of David's fortress, then a name for the whole city and its people. In the Bible it stands for the place God chose to live among his people, and finally for the new city where God and humanity dwell together.
44089: God chose Zion as his resting place.
44091: God installs his king on Zion.
44093: Nations come to learn God's ways.
44095: Being God's city did not protect it from judgement; Jesus weeps over it.
44097: Believers have come to the heavenly Jerusalem; the new Jerusalem comes down from heaven.
44098: From Melchizedek's Salem (Gen 14:18) through David, Solomon's temple, its destruction and rebuilding, and the Songs of Zion in the Psalms.
44099: Jesus is presented there, teaches there, dies outside its walls and rises nearby; the church begins there (Acts 2). Paul contrasts the present Jerusalem and the Jerusalem above.
44100: How these promises relate to the modern city and state of Israel is a live debate among Christians; see /debates/israel-and-church.
44103: Sodom was a city near the Dead Sea that God destroyed with fire in Abraham's day. Ever after it is the Bible's standard example of a society ripe for judgement, and a warning to others, including God's own people.
44105: Its overthrow is the benchmark for devastation.
44107: The prophets shock Judah by calling them Sodom; Ezekiel says Jerusalem was worse.
44109: Genesis describes an attempted gang rape of guests; Ezekiel names pride, plenty, ease and neglect of the poor, plus 'abomination'; Jude speaks of sexual immorality and 'strange flesh'. Some read the core sin as violent inhospitality; others as sexual sin including same-sex acts; many see both. Debated.
44111: Jesus says it will be more bearable for Sodom than for towns that reject him.
44112: Lot settles near Sodom; Abraham intercedes for it (Gen 18:22-33); it becomes a byword in the Law and Prophets.
44113: Jesus, Peter, Jude and Revelation all use Sodom as a warning.
44114: Discussions about sexuality often turn on Sodom; give weight to all the texts together, and note that both sides of the modern debate agree the attempted gang rape was evil.
44117: Eden is the garden home where God placed the first humans. It stands for life as God meant it: plenty, beauty, work with purpose and open friendship with God. Losing Eden pictures what sin lost; its return pictures salvation.
44119: Trees good for food, rivers, work, and God present.
44121: Humans are sent out and cherubim guard the way to the tree of life.
44123: God will make desolate land like Eden.
44124: Garden of God and holy mountain
44125: Ezekiel places Eden on 'the holy mountain of God'.
44126: Fulfilled and surpassed in the new creation
44127: The tree of life and the river return, and the curse is gone.
44128: Genesis 2 to 3, the prophets' images of restored land, and Ezekiel's laments over Tyre and Egypt.
44129: Not named in the New Testament, but echoed in 'paradise' (Luke 23:43; 2 Cor 12:4) and in Revelation 22.
44130: Eden's location is unknown; Genesis names the Tigris and Euphrates alongside two unidentified rivers. How literally to read Genesis 2 to 3 is part of /debates/creation.
44132: The Jordan runs down from the north to the Dead Sea and marked the eastern border of the promised land. Crossing it meant entering the promise. Later it is where John baptised and where Jesus was baptised.
44134: God stops the river so Israel crosses on dry ground, echoing the Red Sea.
44136: Elijah parts the Jordan, is taken up, and Elisha parts it again with his cloak.
44138: Naaman is healed after reluctantly washing seven times in a small, muddy river.
44140: John baptises at the Jordan, the border of the land, suggesting a new entry into God's promise.
44142: Christian hymns and spirituals use crossing Jordan for dying and entering heaven. This is a later devotional image, not a biblical use.
44143: Lot chooses the Jordan plain (Gen 13:10-11); Israel crosses at Gilgal; Elijah and Elisha minister around it; Jeremiah speaks of 'the thicket of the Jordan' (Jer 12:5).
44144: John's baptism, Jesus' baptism and the Spirit descending like a dove, and Jesus' ministry 'beyond the Jordan' (John 10:40).
44146: Sinai (also called Horeb) is the mountain where God met Moses in the burning bush and later gave Israel the covenant and the law. It stands for God's holy, awe-inspiring presence and for the old covenant.
44148: Israel becomes God's treasured people and kingdom of priests.
44150: Fire, smoke, thunder and fear kept the people at a distance.
44152: Elijah meets God at Horeb not in wind, earthquake or fire but in a low whisper.
44154: Paul links Sinai with slavery and Hagar; Hebrews contrasts Sinai's fear with Zion's welcome. Neither denies Sinai's goodness, but both say something greater has come.
44155: The burning bush, the giving of the law, the golden calf, the tabernacle instructions and Elijah's flight. Poetry remembers God 'coming from Sinai' (Deut 33:2; Ps 68:8).
44156: Stephen recalls the angel at Sinai (Acts 7:30-38); Paul and Hebrews use Sinai to explain the old and new covenants.
44157: The mountain's location is debated: the traditional Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai peninsula, other Sinai sites, or a site in north-west Arabia (Paul's 'Mount Sinai in Arabia', Gal 4:25, may mean the Nabataean region, which included Sinai).
44160: 'The nations' (or Gentiles) means all the peoples who were not Israel. They often appear as idol-worshippers and enemies, yet from Abraham onward God promises to bless all nations, and the New Testament describes Gentiles welcomed into God's people as equals.
44162: The table of nations traces all peoples to Noah's sons.
44164: Paul calls this promise the gospel announced in advance.
44166: Israel was not to copy the nations' practices.
44168: Israel's servant is a light to the nations; foreigners will pray in God's house.
44170: Jews and Gentiles become one new people without Gentiles having to become Jews.
44172: The final picture keeps nations distinct but united in worship.
44173: Foreigners such as Rahab, Ruth, Naaman and the Ninevites respond to God, while the nations at large are judged for cruelty and idolatry (Amos 1 to 2).
44174: Jesus' ministry touches Gentiles (Matt 8:10-11); Pentecost gathers people 'from every nation' (Acts 2:5-11), which many see as a reversal of Babel; Paul is the apostle to the Gentiles.
44175: Deuteronomy 32:8 reads 'sons of Israel' in the standard Hebrew text but 'sons of God' in the Dead Sea Scrolls and Greek. Some scholars (for example Michael Heiser) build a view of nations assigned to lesser spiritual powers on this; others are more cautious. Debated.
44177: The hand is how people act, work, hold, give and fight. In the Bible 'the hand of God' means God's power at work, and the right hand, usually the stronger one, means strength, favour and the place of honour.
44179: God brought Israel out 'with a strong hand'; his hand is not too short to save.
44181: No one can snatch Christ's sheep out of the Father's hand; God has engraved his people on his palms.
44183: Jacob crosses his hands to give the right-hand blessing to the younger son; the sheep stand at the King's right.
44187: Raising the hand accompanied a solemn oath.
44188: 'The hand of the LORD came upon' a prophet describes inspiration (Ezek 1:3; 2 Kgs 3:15). Stretching out the hand begins plagues in Egypt.
44189: Jesus heals by touch, takes children in his hands, shows his wounded hands after rising (John 20:27), and sits at the Father's right hand.
44190: God's 'hand' and 'arm' are figures of speech for his action; the Bible also says God is spirit (John 4:24).
44194: Eyes see, notice and desire. God's eyes stand for his watchful care and complete knowledge; human eyes stand for understanding, for desire and for generosity or greed.
44196: Nothing is hidden from God's sight; his eyes are on those who fear him.
44198: 'Open my eyes' is a prayer for understanding.
44200: Sin often begins with seeing and wanting.
44201: Good eye and evil eye: generosity and stinginess
44202: In Hebrew idiom a 'good eye' is generous and an 'evil eye' is grudging. Many scholars read Jesus' 'healthy eye' saying in this light, since it sits between sayings on money; others take it more generally of focused devotion.
44204: God's people are 'the apple of his eye', the pupil a person instinctively protects.
44205: God sees Hagar ('the God who sees', Gen 16:13); doing 'what was right in his own eyes' describes moral chaos (Judg 21:25).
